The framework illustrates how human intent originates from users and creators, researchers and developers, and domain experts; is represented and translated into machine-optimizable objectives; and subsequently influences diffusion model behavior through model-level and generation-level optimization. It further highlights the key trade-offs arising during optimization, including proxy fidelity, diversity–alignment balance, human agency, and system cost. Finally, it summarizes complementary evaluation practices, ranging from automated metrics to human-grounded evaluations, for assessing whether optimization outcomes genuinely align with evolving human intent.. Abstract. Diffusion models are evolving from general tools into personalized systems that adapt to user needs through fine-tuning and guidance. However, diffusion optimization mainly targets measurable objectives such as aesthetics, rarely examining whether they align with human intent. Human needs are multidimensional, contextual, and dynamic, whereas existing methods approximate them with fixed metrics. Because these metrics capture human needs only partially and may amplify deviations from true intent during optimization, higher scores need not yield results better matching human expectations. To understand how human needs enter and influence optimization, we systematically analyze how human intent is expressed, translated into optimizable objectives, applied to model behavior or generation, and evaluated through outputs. We further discuss trade-offs affecting human-intent alignment in personalized image generation and gaps between automated metrics and real user judgments. This human-centered synthesis reorganizes diffusion optimization and provides a systematic reference for personalized generation systems designed for human preferences. Keywords: Human–AI Co-Creation, Human Intent, Human-Centered AI, Generative Model Optimization 1. Introduction Research on diffusion models ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2024 ; Choi et al., 2024 ; Son et al., 2024 ; Dhawka et al., 2024 ; Rajcic et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Kamali et al., 2025 ; Porquet et al., 2025 ) is shifting from “how to generate images” to “how to better meet specific human preferences” ( Wu et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026a ) . In earlier text-to-image paradigms, users expressed intent mainly through prompts, and models generated images accordingly. Recently, fine-tuning ( Black et al., 2024 ) and training-free guidance ( Yan et al., 2026b ) have changed this interaction: generative models no longer merely respond to text prompts, but can adapt their behavior based on human preferences and feedback to optimize toward specific goals ( Black et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2024a ) . Despite these advances, optimizing generative models toward human preferences does not necessarily ensure that their outputs faithfully reflect human intent ( Dang et al., 2025 ) . Human needs are often multidimensional, subjective, and context-dependent, making it difficult to directly translate them into computational objectives and verify whether the resulting images truly satisfy user expectations ( Zhang et al., 2024c ) . Consequently, bridging the gap between human intent and personalized image generation involves three interconnected challenges. (1) User intent must be expressed and translated into computable objectives . User intent must first be externalized through text, choices, ratings, or other forms of feedback, and subsequently translated into machine-optimizable objectives ( Shen et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . Thus, what optimization algorithms actually process is not human intent itself, but a proxy representation constructed from these interaction signals ( Zeng et al., 2024 ; Subramonyam et al., 2024 ) . Different forms of expression capture different aspects of user needs, and the same subjective need may be mapped to different computational objectives, potentially resulting in information loss before intent enters the optimization process ( Mahdavi Goloujeh et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2024 ) . (2) Different user needs must be coordinated as optimization objectives . Personalized generation often involves multiple dimensions, such as aesthetic quality, semantic consistency, realism, and diversity ( Zhang et al., 2024c ; Fan et al., 2024 ) . These dimensions may naturally compete with each other, and their importance can change across tasks and generated results ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Maier et al., 2026 ) . However, existing methods usually combine multiple evaluation objectives in a static way, compressing users’ multidimensional and dynamic needs into optimization signals with fixed weights ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Lee and Choi, 2026 ) . Such preset objective relations are hard to adjust with changing user preferences ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . As a result, the model may keep reinforcing some objectives while sacrificing others that are more important in the current context, causing the optimization direction to deviate from users’ actual preferences ( Jena et al., 2024 ; Hong et al., 2026b ; Amershi et al., 2019 ) . (3) Optimization outcomes must be validated against actual human preferences . Improving predefined optimization objectives does not necessarily mean that generated results better satisfy human needs or align with user intent ( Wadinambiarachchi et al., 2024 ; Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) . Existing studies often evaluate generated outputs using reward scores, text-image alignment, aesthetic metrics, or other automated evaluators, which may share similar assumptions with the objectives used during optimization ( Wiles et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024a ) . Consequently, even when both optimization targets and evaluation metrics improve, it remains unclear whether these improvements correspond to what users actually perceive, prefer, or expect from the generated results ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Naqvi et al., 2025 ) . From a human-centered perspective, evaluating personalized generation requires moving beyond automated metrics to consider human judgments, individual preferences, and the specific contexts in which users interact with generative systems ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2024b ) . For highly subjective and context-dependent needs, the key is therefore not merely to confirm improvements in proxy metrics, but to examine whether these gains translate into greater satisfaction of human preferences and better alignment with users’ actual intentions ( Cao et al., 2025b ) . Together, these three challenges highlight that human intent is not directly mapped to the final output of a generative system; instead, it undergoes a continuous transformation process. Human intent must be represented as machine-optimizable objectives, which are then coordinated and translated into changes in model behavior or generation trajectories ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . Throughout this process, incomplete proxy representations, competing objectives, and optimization mechanisms may introduce tensions and unintended outcomes, potentially weakening alignment with human preferences. Ultimately, whether optimization truly succeeds must be assessed through human-centered validation rather than improvements in automated metrics alone ( Huh et al., 2025 ; Trinh et al., 2025 ) . These interconnected challenges suggest that understanding human-centered diffusion model optimization requires examining not only how optimization is performed, but also how human intent is represented, transformed, potentially distorted, and ultimately evaluated. Therefore, rather than organizing existing studies by algorithm type ( Jiang et al., 2024b ; Cao et al., 2025a ) . This paper re-examines diffusion model optimization through four interconnected dimensions: intent representation, optimization mechanisms, failure modes and trade-offs, and human-centered validation. Based on this perspective, we address the following four research questions: • RQ1: How is human intent represented and operationalized in diffusion model optimization? • RQ2: How do existing optimization paradigms translate human intent into changes in model behavior or generation trajectories? • RQ3: What tensions and failure modes emerge when optimizing diffusion models toward human-defined or human-proxied objectives? • RQ4: How is alignment with human intent validated through automated and human-centered evaluations, and what limitations remain in current evaluation practices? To address these research questions, we systematically review existing studies on diffusion model optimization through a human-centered analytical framework encompassing four interconnected dimensions: intent representation, optimization mechanisms, failure modes and trade-offs, and human-centered validation. Specifically, we investigate how human intent is expressed and translated into machine-optimizable objectives (RQ1), how different optimization paradigms translate these objectives into changes in model behavior or generation trajectories (RQ2), what tensions and failure modes emerge during optimization (RQ3), and how existing evaluation practices assess whether optimization outcomes genuinely align with human preferences and user needs (RQ4). By connecting these dimensions, our review provides a unified perspective on how human intent is represented, operationalized, executed, and validated throughout diffusion model optimization. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • We systematically examine how human intent is expressed, represented, and translated into machine-optimizable objectives, revealing potential information loss and mismatches between user needs and computational proxies. • We organize reinforcement-learning fine-tuning and inference-time optimization into model-level and generation-level paradigms, systematically comparing how they translate human-centered objectives into changes in model behavior or generation trajectories. • We identify key trade-offs and failure modes in human-centered diffusion model optimization, examining how proxy-objective mismatch, competing objectives, reduced diversity, and optimization costs may undermine alignment with human intent. • We systematically examine automated and human-centered evaluation practices, highlighting discrepancies between proxy-based metrics and actual human judgments, and identifying limitations in validating whether optimization outcomes genuinely satisfy user needs. Human Intent in Diffusion Model Optimization Diffusion models ( Smith et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Grace et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Simonen et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Moore et al., 2023 ; Yan et al., 2026e ) generate images through iterative denoising, allowing external signals to influence intermediate states and offering more control than one-shot conditioning. Early classifier and classifier-free guidance show that changing sampling directions can shape outputs and trade off quality, alignment, and diversity. Recently, such control has moved toward preference-driven personalized generation. Some methods update model parameters to change long-term behavior ( Zhao et al., 2022 ; Gan et al., 2024 ; Yan et al., 2026d ; Yan et al., 2026c ) , while others keep parameters fixed and adjust latents or denoising trajectories at inference time. We call them model-level optimization and generation-level optimization . From an HCI view, the key is not only what reward is used, but how human needs enter the system ( Yan et al., 2026f ) . In generative AI, user goals are often clarified through repeated generation, observation, and revision ( Amershi et al., 2019 ; Brade et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024b ) . Prompts are only one expression form and are limited for fine-grained or contextual needs; choices, clicks, and context can further convey intent ( Shen et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2024 ) . Thus, human intent refers to the user’s overall goal for both the desired output and the generation process, while interaction signals are its external representations ( Brade et al., 2023 ) . We define human-centered diffusion model optimization as obtaining goals related to human needs and using them to actively change model behavior or generation trajectories. These needs may come directly from users or through proxy models ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2023 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ; Bansal et al., 2024 ; Yan et al., 2026a ) . 2.2. Human-Centered Diffusion Model Optimization Diffusion model optimization has evolved from improving generation capabilities and controllability toward aligning generated outputs with human preferences and intentions. Early research primarily focused on the fundamental principles and generation capabilities of text-to-image diffusion models ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent studies extended these capabilities through controllable generation, introducing different mechanisms for incorporating specific conditions, multiple constraints, and general control signals into the generation process ( Jiang et al., 2024b ; Cao et al., 2025a ) . While these advances have improved the controllability of diffusion models, they primarily address how generation can be technically controlled rather than whether the resulting outputs genuinely satisfy human needs. More recently, diffusion model optimization has increasingly incorporated human preferences and feedback into the generation process. Research has explored preference modeling, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), direct preference optimization (DPO), and test-time alignment to steer generative models toward human-defined objectives ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . Related studies have examined preference alignment in image generation and editing, highlighting the roles of reward modeling, RLHF, and DPO in adapting generation behavior to human preferences ( Wu et al., 2026b ) . These developments suggest a growing shift from optimizing predefined technical objectives toward incorporating human preferences into model optimization. However, human preferences are often represented through computational proxies, raising questions about whether improvements in these objectives genuinely reflect users’ underlying intentions. From a human-centered computing perspective, effective optimization requires not only improving predefined objectives but also understanding how human intent is expressed, interpreted, and incorporated into generative systems. Prior HCI research emphasizes that user goals are not necessarily fixed or fully specified in advance; instead, they may be progressively clarified and revised through interaction, feedback, and contextual information ( Amershi et al., 2019 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2024 ) . Accordingly, human-centered diffusion model optimization should be understood as a process that connects human intent with computational objectives, uses these objectives to influence model behavior or generation trajectories, and evaluates whether the resulting outputs genuinely satisfy user needs. This perspective moves beyond classifying optimization techniques solely by their technical mechanisms and instead emphasizes how human intent is represented, operationalized, and maintained throughout the optimization process. Human-Centered Evaluation of Generative AI Evaluating generative AI has traditionally relied on automated metrics to assess the quality of generated outputs. In image generation, commonly used measures include visual fidelity, text-image alignment, aesthetic quality, and learned preference scores. These metrics provide scalable and efficient evaluation mechanisms, but their improvements do not necessarily correspond to human perceptions or preferences. Prior research has identified discrepancies between automated metrics and human judgments, highlighting the importance of incorporating human evaluation when assessing text-to-image generation ( Otani et al., 2023 ; Wiles et al., 2025 ) . From a human-centered perspective, evaluation should therefore consider not only measurable output quality but also whether generated results satisfy users’ actual expectations. HCI research has demonstrated that evaluating generative systems requires attention to preferences and interaction contexts. For example, PromptCharm investigates how multimodal prompting and iterative refinement help users generate images that better match their intentions ( Wang et al., 2024b ) . Similarly, RoomDreaming examines personalized design exploration by considering users’ preferences, interaction efficiency, and satisfaction throughout the creative process ( Wang et al., 2024a ) . Collaborative fashion-design systems provide HCI examples of generative AI embedded in multi-stage creative workflows. CrossGAI supports cross-device designer collaboration through AI-assisted sketch retrieval, sketch generation, and sketch-to-image synthesis, whereas HAIGEN integrates text-guided inspiration, personalized sketch-material retrieval, sketch refinement, and coloring ( Deng et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2024a ) . Other studies have shown that AI-generated content can influence users’ creative exploration and decision-making, suggesting that improvements in generation capabilities do not necessarily lead to better interaction experiences ( Wadinambiarachchi et al., 2024 ) . These findings indicate that human-centered evaluation extends beyond assessing generated outputs to understanding how users interact with, interpret, and refine generative results. Meanwhile, the reliability of human evaluation remains a consideration. Human judgments may vary with evaluation criteria, participant backgrounds, and experimental protocols, making evaluation design and reproducibility essential ( Otani et al., 2023 ) . Accordingly, human-centered evaluation requires combining automated measurements with human judgments and contextual assessments to determine whether generative systems support user needs. Existing Surveys and Our Perspective Existing surveys have examined diffusion models from several complementary perspectives. Early reviews primarily focused on the foundations, architectures, and generation capabilities of text-to-image diffusion models ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent surveys extended this scope to controllable generation, systematically organizing existing methods according to control conditions, implementation mechanisms, and evaluation strategies ( Jiang et al., 2024b ; Cao et al., 2025a ) . More recently, research on diffusion model alignment has received increasing attention. Liu et al. ( Liu et al., 2026a ) reviewed alignment objectives, preference modeling, optimization techniques, and evaluation benchmarks, while Wu et al. ( Wu et al., 2026b ) provided a comprehensive analysis of preference alignment in image generation and editing, covering reinforcement learning from human feedback, direct preference optimization, and reward modeling. Together, these surveys establish an important foundation for understanding the technical development of diffusion models and their alignment with human preferences. Despite their complementary contributions, these reviews differ from our work in their primary analytical focus. Existing surveys generally emphasize model capabilities, control mechanisms, optimization paradigms, or alignment techniques, whereas the transformation of human intent across different stages of optimization receives less integrated treatment. In particular, how user needs are expressed through interaction, translated into computational proxies, coordinated as optimization objectives, and subsequently validated against actual human preferences is not typically examined as a unified process. This distinction is important because successful optimization of a predefined objective does not necessarily imply that the resulting generation faithfully reflects the user’s underlying intent, especially when preferences are subjective, multidimensional, and context-dependent. To complement existing surveys, our work adopts human intent transformation as its central analytical perspective. Rather than introducing another taxonomy based primarily on model architectures or optimization algorithms, we connect four interconnected dimensions: intent representation, optimization mechanisms, failure modes and trade-offs, and human-centered validation. This perspective enables us to examine how human needs enter diffusion model optimization, how computational objectives influence model behavior or generation trajectories, where deviations from human intent may emerge, and whether optimization outcomes are genuinely supported by human judgments. By integrating these dimensions into a unified analytical framework, our review provides a human-centered understanding of diffusion model optimization that complements existing technical and preference-alignment surveys. Review Methodology To systematically examine how human intent enters and shapes diffusion model optimization, we conduct a systematic literature review guided by the four research questions. Our methodology consists of three stages: First , we identify and screen relevant studies through cross-database searches, citation tracking, and predefined selection criteria; Second , we extract technical and human-centered information from the selected studies and conduct iterative thematic analysis; Finally , we organize the resulting evidence around four interconnected dimensions: intent representation, optimization mechanisms, failure modes and trade-offs, and human-centered validation. An overview of the systematic review workflow, including study identification, thematic analysis, and the final analytical scope, is presented in Fig . 3 . 3.1. Search and Study Selection We searched studies published between January 2020 and September 2026 on diffusion model optimization, human preferences, and human–AI interaction. The databases included ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, and arXiv, covering HCI, computer vision, machine learning, and generative AI. The search strategy was organized around three concept groups, as summarized in Tab. 3 . The search terms were organized into three concept groups. The first focused on diffusion models, including diffusion model , text-to-image diffusion , and diffusion-based image generation . The second identified optimization mechanisms, including reinforcement learning , RLHF , preference optimization , DPO , reward optimization , training-free guidance , inference/test-time optimization , latent optimization , and trajectory optimization . The third focused on human intent and interaction, including human preference , human feedback , human intent , user preference , alignment , personalization , human-centered , user interaction , interactive generation , iterative refinement , and human-AI co-creation . Since different research communities describe human-centered optimization using different terminology, we did not require studies to explicitly mention human intent or human-centered . Instead, we examined whether their optimization objectives could be meaningfully connected to human needs, preferences, or interaction signals during full-text screening. To reduce omissions caused by keyword variation, we further conducted forward and backward citation tracking on representative studies of reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, preference optimization, training-free guidance, and diffusion alignment, and examined references in related surveys. All studies identified through citation tracking were screened using the same criteria as database results. The selection process included deduplication, title–abstract screening, and full-text assessment. We excluded surveys, opinion articles, tutorials, posters, theses, and short papers without complete method descriptions from the core research corpus; relevant surveys were retained for background analysis and citation tracking. During full-text screening, studies were assessed according to our definition of human-centered diffusion model optimization . Included studies had to satisfy two criteria. First, diffusion models had to serve as the primary generation mechanism, with the proposed method modifying model parameters or the generation process. Second, the optimization objectives had to be directly or indirectly connected to human needs, preferences, or evaluations. Such connections could be established through explicit user feedback, ratings, rankings, pairwise preferences, or computational proxies, including reward and preference models trained on human evaluation data ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) . Importantly, these different forms of human involvement were not treated as equivalent, since computational proxies may capture only selected aspects of the original human intent. Accordingly, we excluded studies focused solely on pretraining, model compression, sampling acceleration, distillation, memory efficiency, or numerical solver efficiency. General conditional or controllable generation was not included simply because it employed textual, positional, or structural conditions, unless these signals further participated in preference-driven optimization. Studies focusing on human–AI interaction, user experience, intent expression, or evaluation without directly optimizing diffusion models were retained as contextual references rather than included in the core corpus. Similarly, works proposing reward models, evaluation metrics, or benchmarks without optimizing diffusion models were used as supplementary evidence for analyzing human-centered evaluation practices. 3.2. Data Extraction and Thematic Analysis For each included study, we extracted information related to human intent, including intent source, expression form, proxy construction, user involvement, and the stage at which human preferences influenced optimization. We also recorded technical characteristics, including publication year, generation task, base model, optimization objectives, intervention mechanisms, and evaluation methods. These variables allowed us to examine both how human needs were operationalized and how the resulting objectives shaped diffusion model optimization. The coding framework was organized around the four research questions. For RQ1, we examined how human intent was expressed, represented, and translated into rewards, preference signals, or other computational proxies. For RQ2, we analyzed how these objectives influenced model behavior or generation trajectories, distinguishing model-level and generation-level optimization . For RQ3, we recorded proxy-objective mismatches, competing objectives, diversity-related trade-offs, optimization costs, and reported failure modes. For RQ4, we extracted automated metrics, human judgments, expert evaluations, and contextual validation methods, with particular attention to whether evaluation practices reflected individual preferences and actual user needs. We then conducted iterative thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and differences across studies. Rather than organizing the literature solely by algorithm type, we compared studies according to how human intent was represented, how optimization objectives were applied, what tensions emerged, and how alignment outcomes were evaluated. Related codes were grouped into broader themes, while distinctions in intent sources, proxy construction, and optimization intervention points were preserved. Ambiguous cases were revisited to refine the coding categories and maintain consistent interpretation across the research corpus. 3.3. Final Corpus and Analytical Scope The final research corpus covered two main pathways through which human-centered objectives influence diffusion model optimization. Model-level optimization updates model parameters to incorporate human preferences into generation behavior, enabling relatively persistent adaptation across subsequent generations. In contrast, generation-level optimization keeps the base model fixed and adjusts the current generation process through guidance, latent optimization, or trajectory intervention. These pathways differ not only in their optimization mechanisms but also in how human intent influences generation behavior and when users can intervene. Since some studies involved multiple mechanisms, we categorized them according to their primary intervention points and the ways in which optimization objectives were applied, without treating the two pathways as mutually exclusive. Rather than organizing the corpus solely by algorithm type, we structured the analysis around the four research questions. Specifically, we first examine how human intent is expressed, represented, and operationalized into computational objectives (RQ1). We then analyze how these objectives influence model behavior or generation trajectories through different optimization mechanisms (RQ2). Next, we investigate the trade-offs, tensions, and failure modes that may emerge when optimizing toward human-defined or human-proxied objectives (RQ3). Finally, we examine how automated and human-centered evaluation practices validate whether optimization outcomes genuinely align with human preferences and user needs (RQ4). Together, these dimensions provide a unified analytical scope for understanding how human intent is represented, executed, potentially distorted, and evaluated throughout diffusion model optimization.
